newsitem.title: USA: Foreign crude business to U.S. quiet, Brent weak.
newsitem.headline: Foreign crude business to U.S. quiet, Brent weak.

text.p: Foreign crude business to the U.S. was subdued on Tuesday, with much talk focused on the availability of overseas crude in the first decade of April.

U.S. domestic sweet crude grades rose sharply on sentiment there was a lack of West African and Brent coming to the U.S. Gulf for early April. Traders said although the outlook for offerings looked heavy for mid-April and later in the month, there was a gap allowing the rise in Louisiana crudes.
"The arbitrage is open, but the offerings are really padded back to later in the month. It looks like all the Glencore Brent has been digested for now," said a trader.
Physical Brent traded earlier in London time at weaker prices, pushing the offerings in the U.S. Gulf lower.
"There's plenty of Brent on offer in the Gulf. In April we're hearing it at about 70-80 cents under," said a trader.
The pair of wet Brents sold earlier for March 26-28 at May Brent minus 68 cents, and March 28-30 at minus 70 cents.
Traders said besides a few other North Sea trades, the wet side of business was stilted.
"Maybe it's because people are traveling back from the NPRA's (National Petroleum Refiners Association) in San Antonio, but we haven't heard anything today," said a broker.
Paper market deals in the U.S. aftermarket window deflated May Brent 10-16 cents from the IPE settlement, with May/June inter-month spreads moving out as well.
Partials deals were abundant for May Brent at $20.15 and $20.12, with more than than the eqivalent of two full cargoes trading hands in a series of transactions.
